ta-l1d15q1-d1e3498.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 15. Having shown that the Spirit proceeds temporally and is given by Father and Son, Lombard asks whether he is also given or sent by himself. He shows that he is, from Augustine and two arguments: whatever Father and Son can do or work, the Spirit can do or work too. Thomas notes that these arguments are effective because of the effect connoted in creatures by mission, since power and operation toward creatures are common to the three. Lombard then compares the Son's mission: how it is understood, by whom he is sent (by the Father, by the Spirit, and by himself, with the objection 'I have not come of myself'), and whether he was sent once or often. Three inquiries are announced: on mission in itself, on the side of the one sent, and on the side of the sender. The first has two articles: whether mission or giving belongs to the divine persons, and whether it signifies the essence or a notion.
claims: The Spirit is given and sent also by himself, since power and operation toward creatures are common to the three.
The Son is sent by the Father, by the Spirit, and by himself.
concepts: mission of the Son and Spirit

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3538.summary: First objection that mission does not belong to divine persons. Mission implies a change of place, as a messenger is sent somewhere, and no change of place fits the omnipresent persons.
claims: Mission implies local change.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3541.summary: Second objection from Jerome on Ezekiel 16:53: what is joined and bound in one body cannot be sent. One divine person is joined to another more closely than any bodily union.
claims: What is united cannot be sent.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3550.summary: Third objection. Nothing implying inferiority can be said of one person relative to another, since there are no grades in the Trinity; Damascene says Christ obeys the Father only as man. Mission and giving seem to imply inferiority in the one sent or given.
claims: Mission implies inferiority of the one sent.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3554.summary: Fourth objection. A divine person is infinitely worthier than any angel, and the higher, assisting angels are not sent to us because of their dignity (Dionysius), so divine persons are much less sent.
claims: The highest angels are not sent because of their dignity.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3557.summary: Notes the many authorities of Scripture and the saints cited in Lombard's text to the contrary.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3560.summary: Thomas's determination. By its signification, mission or giving implies the going out of the one sent from a sender and toward some terminus. In creatures this going out is by bodily distance from the sender and, relative to the terminus, implies that the one sent comes to be where it was not before. Since all imperfection must be removed in divine predication, mission in God is understood not as a going out by local distance or as something new in the one sent, but as a going out of origin from someone as from a principle, and as something new in the one to whom the mission is made, so that the person sent is said to be in it in a new way. Mission thus differs from procession and giving. Procession implies real distinction and relation to its principle, not to a terminus. Giving implies distinction of the given not from its principle, since one can give oneself, but only from the recipient. Mission implies distinction of the one sent both from the principle and from the terminus. So when the Spirit is said to be sent, both relations are included: the eternal, as he proceeds from Father and Son, and the temporal, as he is signified in relation to the creature that stands toward him in a new way.
claims: Mission in God is a going out of origin from a principle together with a new mode of presence in the recipient.
Mission implies distinction from both sender and terminus, unlike procession or giving.
Mission includes both the eternal relation of origin and the temporal relation to the creature.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3563.summary: Reply to the first objection. Although the omnipresent Spirit cannot be where he was not before by a change of place in himself, he can be there in a way he was not before, by a change in that in which he is said to be, and this preserves the meaning of mission.
claims: Mission involves a new mode of presence by a change in the recipient, not in the person.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3566.summary: Reply to the second objection. Jerome's gloss concerns the mission of a creature by change of place, which applies only to what is locally separated. For divine mission the distinction of persons in unity of essence suffices.
claims: Divine mission requires only distinction of persons, not separation.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3569.summary: Reply to the third objection. Obedience properly concerns a command, which belongs to lordship, so obedience implies a grade of dignity and cannot be said of the Son or Spirit in their divinity. Sending, however, implies not a grade of dignity but the authority of principle in one with respect to another who goes out from him, and this order exists among the divine persons.
claims: Sending implies authority of origin, not superiority of dignity, unlike obedience.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3573.summary: Reply to the fourth objection. Mission is not said of an angel and a divine person in the same sense. A sent angel moves locally, being where it was not, since when in heaven it is not on earth, so such mission implies some lack of dignity or lower grade. Mission of a divine person excludes all change of place. Moreover, the effect to which a divine person is sent, sanctifying grace, is from that person immediately, whereas the higher angels' effects reach us through the lower angels (Dionysius). So the higher angels are not said to be sent to us, only the lower ones who act on us immediately, just as a divine person is not sent by the perfections creatures receive from God through some created intermediary.
claims: Divine mission excludes local motion and is to an effect produced immediately by the person.
Higher angels are not sent because their effects reach us through lower angels.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3585.summary: First argument that mission signifies a notion. Bede says the Spirit's mission is his procession, and procession is notional.
claims: Bede identifies mission with procession.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3588.summary: Second argument. Whatever implies origin in God is notional, since the essence neither originates nor is originated, and mission implies a going out of origin from another as from a principle.
claims: Whatever implies origin is notional.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3591.summary: Contrary argument. According to Dionysius every name said of God that connotes an effect in creatures pertains to the common essence, and mission implies an effect in creatures.
claims: Names connoting effects in creatures are essential.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3595.summary: Second contrary argument. No notion is common to Son and Spirit, but mission is common to both, since both are said to be sent.
claims: No notion is common to Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3598.summary: Thomas's determination. Some divine names signify only the person (Father, Son), some only the essence ('essence'), and some both, like the powers of begetting and spirating. Mission is essential and notional in different respects: notional by the relation it implies to its principle, essential by the relation it implies to its effect in the creature. Some hold that it signifies the notion principally and the essence consequently through the connoted effect; others hold the reverse, which Thomas thinks truer given the force of the word. By its name, mission does not imply going out from someone as the principle from which the one sent has being; it implies the authority of someone over the one sent only in ordering to the effect of the mission. A servant sent by his master does not come from him in his being but from a principle moving him by command to this act. Because among the divine persons there can be authority over the one sent only by origin of being, mission consequently implies a relation of origin, by which it is notional, while it principally implies ordering to the effect, by which it is essential. Temporal procession is the reverse: in God it implies going out from an originating principle and implies ordering to the effect only consequently, as to its temporal mode. So temporal procession is principally notional and signifies the essence consequently, through the connoted effect. Thomas adds that one of these terms comes closer to the essence than mission, as is clear from what has been said; the referent of 'hic' is not explicit in the text.
claims: Mission is both essential (by its effect) and notional (by its relation of origin).
Mission principally signifies ordering to its effect and consequently a relation of origin; temporal procession is the reverse.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3601.summary: This resolves the first three arguments.

ta-l1d15q1-d1e3604.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. A notion can be signified in God properly, like paternity or innascibility, or commonly, like 'being from another' or 'from whom another is'. Mission signifies a notion in the latter way, so it is common to the two persons who are from another.
claims: Mission signifies a notion commonly, as 'being from another', shared by Son and Spirit.

ta-l1d15q1-Dd1e3493.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 15 maps Lombard's argument that the Spirit is also sent by himself and his comparison with the Son's mission by the Father, by the Spirit, and by himself. It notes that these arguments work because operation toward creatures is common to the three, and it announces inquiries into mission in itself, from the side of the one sent, and from the side of the sender.
claims: The persons' operation toward creatures is common, so each person can be said to send.

ta-l1d15q1-Dd1e3530.summary: Article 1 asks whether mission belongs to the divine persons. Thomas holds that it does, understood without imperfection: as a going out of origin from a principle and a new mode of presence in the recipient, not local motion or novelty in the one sent. Mission differs from procession, which is related only to the principle, and from giving, which is distinct only from the recipient, since mission is distinct from both sender and terminus. It includes both the eternal and the temporal relation. Divine mission implies authority of origin, not inferiority, and differs from angelic mission, being to an effect, sanctifying grace, produced immediately by the person sent.
claims: Mission belongs to the divine persons as origin from a principle plus a new presence in the creature.
Mission implies authority of origin, not inferiority.

ta-l1d15q1-Dd1e3577.summary: Article 2 asks whether mission signifies the essence or a notion. Thomas holds that it signifies both: principally the ordering to its effect, which is essential, and consequently the relation of origin, which is notional, since among divine persons authority over the one sent can only be by origin. Temporal procession is the reverse. As a notion, mission signifies 'being from another' in a common way and so belongs to both Son and Spirit.
claims: Mission is principally essential and consequently notional; temporal procession is principally notional.
Mission is a common notion of the persons who are from another.

ta-l1d15q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 15 treats divine mission in itself. Article 1 holds that mission belongs to the divine persons, purified of local motion and inferiority. It is a going out of origin from a principle together with a new mode of the person's presence in the creature, so it includes both the eternal relation and the temporal one. It is distinguished from procession and giving, and from angelic mission, by being directed to an effect produced immediately by the person sent. Article 2 holds that 'mission' signifies principally the essential ordering to its effect and consequently the notional relation of origin, which it signifies in a common way shared by Son and Spirit.
claims: Divine mission is origin from a principle together with a new presence in the creature, without inferiority.
Mission signifies principally the essence (through its effect) and consequently a notion common to Son and Spirit.
